newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe 1996/97 budget deficit seen off target.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe 1996/97 budget deficit seen off target.

text.p: Zimbabwe's budget deficit is likely to be higher than an 8.5 percent of gross domestic product target the government was aiming at in the 1996/97 financial year ending June 30, Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa has said.

Murerwa told the Zimbabwe Economic Society on Tuesday evening that recent pay awards to civl servants which were not forecast in the 1996/97 wage bill might make it difficult for the government to cut the deficit to 8.5 percent of GDP in 1996/97 from 10.1 percent in 1995/96.

"As you are aware, the budget deficit for the 1995/96 financial year was 10.1 percent and government has undertaken to reduce it to 8.5 percent during 1996/97. This may be difficult to achieve given the recent wage increases," Murerwa said.

The government of President Robert Mugabe in September awarded its 180,000 civil servants a 20 percent pay rise after the majority of them went on a three-week strike which crippled key social services.
The pay hike was over and above a nine percent increase the civil servants received in July but rejected as inadequate.
Murerwa could not be drawn into saying how much the additional wage bill would be, how the government would finance it and what the budget deficit was likely to be.

But local economic analysts estimated the extra wage bill at Z$1.4 billion (U.S.$130.3 million) and said if the government borrowed this sum from the domestic market it would push the budget deficit to between 10 and 12.5 percent in 1996/97.

Murerwa said the government would continue taking measures to try and reduce its spending and the budget deficit, both essential goals for it to secure International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other Western donor aid for a new programme of economic reforms it planned to launch next year.

The IMF and the World Bank -- which marshalled Western donor aid for the southern African country's first five-year economic reform programme which ended in 1995 -- withheld some aid to Zimbabwe last year after the government failed to meet some cost- saving targets.
Economic analysts blame state overexpenditure, which eats up about 40 percent of GDP, for keeping the budget deficit high and fuelling annual inflation.
The IMF, the World Bank and other international donors say they will only help Zimbabwe's new reform programme after seeing progress in state spending cuts. ($1 = 10.74)
